q.intro.text: A square patio is covered with sixty-four square tiles, each one foot on a side. Its area is sixty-four square feet.

q.ask.text: How long is one side of the patio?

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: The sixty-four tiles fit exactly in a square: no tile left over, no gap.

e.s2.text: Count the tiles along the top edge: eight. Each tile is one foot, so one side is eight feet.

e.s3.text: Check by squaring: eight rows of eight tiles is eight times eight, sixty-four. The area comes back.

e.s4.text: The square root of sixty-four is eight. The square root of the area is the side. The root sign asks: which number times itself makes sixty-four?

e.why.text: Quick check: why is the side eight feet?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. Squaring the side gives back the area, and that is exactly what a square root means.

e.w-half.text: Halving three times lands on eight here by luck. For thirty-six it gives four and a half, but the side is six, because six times six is thirty-six. The real reason is eight times eight is sixty-four.

e.w-perim.text: The four sides add up to eight plus eight plus eight plus eight, thirty-two feet: that is the distance around. The sixty-four counts the tiles inside: eight rows of eight.

t.intro.text: A bigger square patio has an area of one hundred forty-four square feet. The tiles are laid for you. The rest is your turn.

t.count.text: Count the tiles along the top edge. How long is one side?

t.fill.text: Type a number in the box first.

t.c-ok.text: Yes: twelve tiles along the edge, so one side is twelve feet.

t.c-half.text: Seventy-two is half of one hundred forty-four. Count the tiles along the top edge instead.

t.c-perim.text: Thirty-six is one hundred forty-four shared by four sides, as if it were the distance around. But one hundred forty-four counts the tiles inside. Count the tiles along one edge.

t.c-other.text: Count the tiles along the top edge, one by one.

t.check.text: Now check by squaring. How many tiles do twelve rows of twelve make?

t.k-ok.text: Yes: twelve times twelve is one hundred forty-four. The area comes back, so twelve is right.

t.k-double.text: Twelve times two is twenty-four: that doubles the side. Squaring is twelve times twelve: twelve rows of twelve.

t.k-other.text: Twelve times twelve is one hundred twenty, plus twenty-four. Count it again, row by row.

t.write.text: Now write it with the root sign. Tap the numbers into the boxes.

t.w-ok.text: Yes: the square root of one hundred forty-four is twelve. The area goes under the sign; the side is its value.

t.w-swap.text: That is swapped. The area, one hundred forty-four, goes under the root sign; the side, twelve, is the value.

t.w-half.text: Seventy-two is half of one hundred forty-four, and seventy-two times seventy-two is far more than that. The value of the root is the side.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you said eight feet, and you were right. Now you can show why: eight times eight is sixty-four, so the square root of sixty-four is eight.

t.cb-half.text: At the start you picked thirty-two feet, half of sixty-four. But thirty-two times thirty-two is one thousand and twenty-four. The square root of sixty-four is eight, because eight times eight is sixty-four.

t.cb-perim.text: At the start you picked sixteen feet: sixty-four shared by four sides. But sixty-four is the area, not the distance around. The square root of sixty-four is eight.

t.cb-none.text: At the start: a patio of sixty-four square feet has sides of eight feet, because eight times eight is sixty-four.

p.intro.text: Sam notices that the square root of four is two, and four divided by two is also two. Sam says: taking the square root is the same as dividing by two.

p.build-wrong.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.build-right.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.c1.text: Right: two times two is four, so the side is two. Half of four is two as well. Here the two rules agree.

p.c2.text: But four times four is sixteen, so the square root of sixteen is four. Half of sixteen is eight, and a side of eight needs sixty-four tiles: far too many.

p.c3.text: One counterexample is enough: sixteen breaks Sam's rule.

p.x-differ.text: They can agree: at four both give two, and at zero both give zero. Agreeing at a few numbers does not make two rules the same.

p.x-examples.text: Checking a few cases can't prove always. One case that fails is enough to break it.

p.x-slot.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. Taking a square root is not halving.
